A detailed investigation into the statistical characteristics of the Initial Exit Time (IET) in SFD has been conducted. Through an examination of multiple image datasets from the U. of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign's Sole File Diffusion (SFD) tool, we determined the empirical duration statistics. These statistics include maximum entropy distributions, which we categorized as a sum of a uniform distribution and a power-law distribution. A thorough analysis revealed that these duration statistics are consistent across various image types. Additionally, we found a significant correlation between a parameter of the power-law distribution and another parameter of a similar distribution identified by other researchers. Moreover, we discovered that the maximum entropy probabilities associated with IET are directly related to the image resolution. These findings have significant implications for the security of encryption methods, as well as potential avenues for further decryption of secret images.

The traditional understanding that a quantum system's state collapses to an eigenstate following a measurement holds true under specific assumptions. Nevertheless, a recent study challenges this notion by demonstrating its incompatibility with the superposition principle in certain scenarios involving sequential measurements. Building upon this research, a quantum extension of Bayes' theorem has been developed. The application of this theorem clarifies the conditions under which the eigenvalue state remains coherent within the framework of sequential measurements. Furthermore, the theorem underscores the importance of quantum coherence in such situations.

The transition from the ordinary QCD model to the quark-meson model involves replacing the effective potential with the quark field, then applying the high-temperature and high-density expansion to connect this model with the QCD model. This process enables a study of the Formula of State for quark-matter using the quark-meson effective potential with quark and meson degrees of freedom.

Let $H^*(X)$ be the mod 2 cohomology algebra of an arbitrary space $X$. Building upon previous work of Bousfield, specifically that $H^*(X)$ has only finitely many non-simple components, we demonstrate that $H^*(X)$ possesses at most 280 such components.

A new prototype optical screen has been engineered to expand the capabilities of astronomical imaging by enhancing transmission in the Lyman band while maintaining high rejection rates across other wavelengths. Composed of alternating layers of magnesium fluoride and silicon dioxide, the screen's structure can be fine-tuned to narrow its passband,从而提高 spatial resolution in the Lyman-alpha band without compromising color information. Its compact and versatile design allows it to function within both telescopes and laboratory settings, and can also contribute to the development of advanced imaging cameras. Further research has enabled the screen to support high-speed imaging at rates of up to 10 kHz.

In a confined area of wireless communication, devices such as perfect waveguides can be employed as management tools to shape electromagnetic fields. Utilizing the concept of graph Ising models, we analyze how these devices affect networks of wires depicted as two-sided graphs. Our research shows that symmetrical graph devices can be used to solve the maximum clique problem within these networks through ideal management, effectively transforming original graphs into modified versions with the same number of nodes and connections. Our study also involves creating graph devices by fusing wires and examining their effects on network symmetries and clusters. Ultimately, we propose a network design framework where graph devices are used to induce varying levels of order within networks of wires.

Over the past two decades, major astronomical surveys have greatly expanded the size of publicly available data sets, increasing their size tenfold to hundreds of gigapixels. To manage and analyze vast amounts of astronomical data, researchers have developed groundbreaking cataloging tools. These systems not only help researchers quickly locate objects but also significantly improve measurement accuracy and streamline the process of matching data across different surveys. Despite significant advancements, cataloging processes are still largely labor-intensive and time-consuming, requiring manual intervention. In this paper, a pioneering approach to automated cataloging is presented, utilizing deep learning techniques to create accurate cataloging layers. These layers are then optimized through graph cuts to produce a comprehensive catalog, which can be easily adapted to various existing systems and applied to real-world datasets.

This paper introduces a code-based authentication system utilizing weak error-correcting codes over Gallager channels, specifically targeting low error rates. Traditional channel decoding methods, like maximum likelihood, maximum a posteriori, and minimum distance decoding, are ineffective in this context due to excessive computational demands and unsuitability for real-time applications. To address this limitation, the paper explores random linear checksum decoding (R-LCD), a technique that achieves near-optimal performance while maintaining efficiency through parallel processing and linear time complexity at high success rates. Building on this foundation, a new keyless authentication protocol based on repeated random linear checksum decoding (R-RLCD) is developed, yielding improved error correction capabilities compared to existing systems while retaining parallel processing efficiency. Furthermore, the paper derives a closed-form expression for the success probability of repeated random linear checksum decoding, facilitating the optimization of repetition degree and, in turn, enhancing the overall performance of the proposed keyless authentication system compared to established alternatives.

Sudden acceleration of an oscillating particle in a periodic potential yields significant effects on its dynamics when the acceleration is high relative to friction. The particle exhibits distinct responses to different levels of acceleration, including dispersion-free and dispersion-rich movements. This phenomenon occurs because the particle in the dispersion-free regime traverses flat sections of the potential's profile, but a further increase in acceleration causes the particle to jump directly from one dispersion-rich region to another, skipping over the areas where it would have exhibited localized oscillations.

When assessing shock impacts, such as in policy transmission or economic growth, impulse response analysis provides valuable non-recurrent effects. In recent years, a new technique called local projections (LP) has gained popularity for this purpose due to its simplicity and theoretical robustness. This study introduces an innovative variation of LP that enhances its ability to capture nuanced changes by making the predictor endogenous. Simulations and real-world applications to LSE's business forecast data demonstrate that this adaptable LP method outperforms both conventional LP and time-varying parameter models in forecasting accuracy.

A non-zero, entropy-inducing quantum fluctuation arising from rotational symmetry breaking, known as the angular Casimir entropy, is studied. This phenomenon occurs in a Landau gauge as a free point charge and is proposed as a new electromagnetic self-interaction. The electrostatically induced angular Casimir angle is calculated for the system.

A crucial aspect of analysis and understanding in hyperbolic structured data is Named Entity Classification (NEC), which is an essential task for building human-like machines. However, the majority of existing studies on NEC overlook the fact that hierarchical data forms a non-Euclidean geometry and instead treat it as if it were in Euclidean space, often using traditional methods such as the highly computationally expensive K-means clustering algorithm. In response, this study proposes a new framework, FGNET-RH, for detailed named entity classification in hierarchical datasets that operates within a hyperbolic geometry. The proposed framework leverages a subalgebra to represent and measure distances between nodes in this geometry and then uses a network to learn and capture common patterns in the data, thereby facilitating accurate NEC. The effectiveness of the proposed framework is demonstrated through its superior performance over its existing counterparts on two real-world subaltree datasets, which are designed for the study of amphibian and mammalian classification systems.

The paper investigates two types of second Hankel determinants, one involving the class $\mathcal{U}$ and the other $\mathcal{S}_2^0$, yielding the lower bounds $H_2 \ge 4$ and $H_2 \ge 8$ for the respective determinants. Furthermore, various sufficient criteria are introduced to ensure the eighth power of the series in class $\mathcal{U}$ falls within $\mathcal{U}$ and the series in class $\mathcal{S}$ meets subgroup conditions.

Optimal allocation of virtual machines within a cloud data center is critical for minimizing costs, reducing energy consumption, and preventing overloading. However, the dynamic nature of cloud services makes it difficult to forecast traffic patterns accurately. As a result, many servers experience uneven distribution of computational loads. To tackle this issue, we developed Prepartition, an innovative load distribution approach for a large-scale cloud data center hosting diverse cloud services. Our experiment demonstrated that Prepartition effectively reduces the average number of servers per node from 10.9 to 9.1, representing a 17% decrease in overprovisioning. Our code is available on GitHub at github.com/berkeleylab/prepartition for review and testing purposes.

In many economic environments, outcomes ultimately settle into a game-theoretic equilibrium. However, achieving this equilibrium can be challenging. Research indicates that players' behavior sometimes deviates from the predicted rational strategies, especially when playing in repeated games or games with similar structures. To address this discrepancy, our study focuses on enhancing a model called Fixed Point Networks (FPNs), which forecasts game equilibria from learned patterns. FPNs, trained on actual and simulated data, show a notable propensity for deviating from equilibrium states. To rectify this limitation, we incorporate the concept of experience replay into FPNs, allowing the networks to revisit and reassess past experiences. Our results demonstrate that this experience replay mechanism significantly improves FPNs' adherence to equilibrium states, particularly in complex environments.

A new statistical technique has been developed to quantify the potential effects on a variable when other parameters are altered. This method utilizes data from a control group and creates a theoretical experimental group where applicable control parameters are freely varied, resulting in the generation of an optimal treatment assignment scheme based on simulated proxy outcomes. By utilizing an unbiased estimator to measure the experiment's potential impact and establishing the theoretical lower bound of this bound, a hypothesis test can be conducted to determine if the experiment's potential impact is significantly different from zero. This unconfoundedness assumption-based test has the potential to be more accurate than traditional regression techniques. Additionally, a simulation has been conducted to demonstrate the method's effectiveness in scenarios with a large number of control and experimental parameters.

This study examines the vulnerability of a critical infrastructure system to hidden attacks that cause damage without being noticed. To protect such a system, we aim to design better monitoring techniques and covert attacks to identify and manipulate system behavior. Specifically, we're interested in understanding how certain actions and biases within the system affect its detectability and estimation. By re-framing these concerns as optimization problems, we can either discover covert attacks that go undetected for extended periods, or determine the most effective monitoring parameters to minimize bias in our estimates. Our approach relies on representing these problems using quadratic functions that account for covert attacks and process noise biases, allowing us to use optimized solution methods to generate actionable insights. In so doing, we expand upon existing research and provide a more comprehensive understanding of how certain actions and biases within the system affect its security and reliability.

We introduce GAE-ISumm, a universal Chinese-based summarization model, uniquely tailored for summarizing crucial religious texts in various Indian languages. Operating in a entirely unsupervised setting, it leverages a carefully designed network architecture and novel training components without necessitating manual annotations. GAE-ISumm is the first of its kind, optimized for multilingual text summarization across diverse Indian languages such as Bengali, Gujarati, Hindi, Kannada, Marathi, and Tamil, thereby eliminating reliance on large training datasets typically required. Our experiments demonstrate that, on average, GAE-EISumm yields a 1.6-point improvement in ROUGE scores over several established English and non-Indian language-based summarization models, signifying its superior performance. Furthermore, evaluations conducted by both established human metrics (ROUGE, METEOR, CIDEr, and RWG) and advanced large language models (GPT-3.5-Turbo and LLaMA-2-70B) confirm the enhanced summarization capabilities of GAE-EISumm. The model and accompanying data can be freely accessed via the following URL: https://github.com/DeepLearning-Indore/VLLM/tree/main/VLLM/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/VADER/V

We explore the structural properties of s-rings of Noether type within Groshniev's Grothendieck category $\mathcal{G}$, focusing on the definition and characterization of these s-rings with unit and their connection to group categories.

A recent study identified a hidden population of M giant stars exhibiting a weak form of acceleration in the Milky Way's disk. These stars display characteristic movement patterns, suggesting they are likely influenced by the gravitational pull of a hidden companion. By analyzing a subset of these affected stars, we have calculated the probability distributions of their binary companion's properties. Our findings indicate that the companion systems have a median distance of around 100 astronomical units and a range of mass ratios favoring heavier primary stars. By comparing our results to previous studies of normal stellar populations, we discover significant differences in the mass-separation relationships, which may be attributed to the mass loss that occurs during a star's evolution. Our findings also suggest that the population of companion systems has a lower separation limit than previously thought, which is consistent with the predicted disruption of shorter-period orbits due to mass loss.

In unsupervised feature learning, deep autoencoders serve a critical role, but they tend to learn meaningless features due to an inherent identity mapping solution. To address this issue, several regularization techniques have been developed. Although some methods apply constraints to ensure features have a specific statistical distribution, they rely on assumptions that may not hold. Conversely, the Variational Bayesian Autoencoder (AVE) automatically discovers the distribution of hidden data through parameter estimation. The minimum square AVE further enforces this by penalizing the mean squared reconstruction error. However, the EM algorithm used for learning is sensitive to initial conditions and converges slowly. To enhance these models, a new algorithm called the Variational Autoencoder with Constraint (CAVE) is proposed, utilizing a minimum square constraint for hidden data. CAVE combines Bayesian inference with the fast-converging IRLS algorithm, making it more effective. Experimental results demonstrate that CAVE achieves superior performance in terms of reconstruction and leads to more informative features, as evidenced by better results in a letter recognition task.

Integrating the Internet of Things (IoT) into everyday life has become a significant focus for researchers and engineers worldwide, with smart home technology as a pivotal area of study. As part of their quest to develop innovative IoT applications, scholars and engineers have been working on private blockchain and indoor positioning systems, aiming to integrate the two for enhanced smart home solutions. A promising approach involves integrating private blockchain with IoT for security purposes, enabling data transfer and network management within localized, trusted networks. By incorporating indoor positioning systems into IoT-enabled smart homes, devices can automatically execute predetermined tasks based on user locations, thus boosting user satisfaction through streamlined, intelligent home management. In this paper, researchers have explored the potential of integrating private blockchain and indoor positioning systems in smart home tracking solutions, leveraging innovative IoT-enabled home management strategies.

This research introduces an advanced method to enhance the performance of 
quantized cell-free networks, specifically by accurately modeling the 
transmission characteristics of 3D channel vectors. A neural network is used 
to approximate the L-norm (L1 or Euclidean) thetawrap quantization function at 
each user terminal. The network takes the channel conditions, channel samples, and 
the actual distance distribution as input, and the result is incorporated as an 
adjustment factor in the quantized cell-free network's channel representation. 
The proposed method is particularly suitable for applications where phase 
quantization schemes are used, and the researchers also demonstrate its 
effectiveness in quantizing angle of arrival. The analysis shows that the novel 
approach results in significant improvements in sum-rate performance compared to 
alternative methods.

We have developed two parameterized algorithms for testing and drawing directed graphs in an upward planar format.  Firstly, we created an algorithm running in time O*((w^3)) where w represents the graph's width, and this was achieved by parameterizing the problem based on graph width and treewidth.  Then, we established a kernel consisting of at most O(k^2) vertices for treewidth treators, and this resulted in an O*((w^3)) algorithm.  Finally, we parameterized the problem based on the treewidth and produced a fixed-parameter tractable algorithm for it.

In recent years, there has been a surge in the availability of large-scale, crowdsourced data sets. To derive meaningful insights from these data sets, sophisticated ensemble modeling techniques have been developed and refined. This report presents a novel ensemble modeling method that is specifically tailored to analyze noisy crowdsourced data. The proposed approach incorporates insights from the diversity of human responses as measured by a Monte Carlo simulation. The results of this research show that integrating the diversity of human feedback enhances the accuracy and reliability of ensemble models in predicting complex systems, such as the behavior of autonomous vehicles. The novel method has also been applied to a wide range of applications, including the prediction of human movement in crowds, the behavior of social networks, and the evolution of cultural practices.

For semiflows on compact manifolds, particularly in cases where the transfer operators exhibit rapid mixing, we demonstrate a significant decrease in the norm of $(s+t)$-th powers of pseudo-holomorphic and anisotropic transfer operators, compared to the product of $s$-th and $t$-th powers of their absolute values.

A covering array with tiny strength $2$ is a specialized matrix, often called a CTA-Matrix, composed of symbols from a limited set. Each pair of columns contains all possible combinations of these symbols an equal number of times, a property achieved by leveraging existing covering arrays. Researchers have developed methods to establish both lower and upper bounds on the minimum size of such matrices, exploring the maximum size possible within given constraints.

In a game involving two parties, with strategies limited to $d$-dimensional states, and where payoffs are determined by the difference of a function of the joint state and the local states, it has been proven under certain conditions, namely when the joint state is a noisy version of a maximally entangled state and the function used is symmetric and monotone under transformations, that a unique optimal pure strategy pair exists and is unique in the entire set of mixed strategies. Furthermore, under the same conditions but with no entanglement, a unique optimal pure strategy pair also exists when $d$ is even or when one dimension is $2$ and the other is odd. However, in the absence of entanglement, if either one dimension is $2$ and the other is odd or both dimensions are greater than $2$, no universally pure strategy exists that applies to all functions used in the joint state function.

A directed genetic algorithm is being evaluated in an automated framework designed to uncover the root causes of software failures. The framework utilizes a genetic algorithm to streamline a directed action approach, which aims to establish a connection between observed symptoms and underlying root causes. By applying a fitness function based on this directed framework, our study seeks to isolate the influence of specific factors: the framework itself, root cause models, and root cause representations. However, due to discrepancies between initial study parameters and our available project data, our results indicate that the framework generally yields positive outcomes, yet frequently falls short in identifying root causes with high precision. Furthermore, our findings highlight the importance of accurate fault tree construction, which often requires manual verification. Consequently, future enhancements could prioritize refining the framework, improving fault tree models, and developing more effective root cause representations.

The interplay between interactions and kinematics in high-temperature superconductors remains a complex issue.
Within a $t$-$J$ model framework, theoretical studies suggest a significant shift in the preferred shape of vortices in the mixed-phase as toffee value increases from 4 to 8.
This shift could potentially explain the varied vortex morphology observed across the superconducting region of a phase diagram.
To examine this concept, we have analyzed the shape of vortices in a single-crystal sample of $\textrm{La}_{2-x}\textrm{Sr}_x\textrm{CuO}_4$ with $x = 0.065$, operating near $t^*/t \approx 6$.
Through high-resolution analysis using SQUID microscopy, we found that both rectangular and square shapes can be identified among the vortices.
This discovery aligns with predictions regarding a square-to-square $\times 2$ rectangular grid transition.
This phenomenon might be a general feature in $\textrm{La}_{2-x}\textrm{Sr}_x\times \textrm{CuO}_4$ and other cuprate superconductors.

Researchers have discovered a method to study the anisotropic flow of thermal photons in quark-gluon plasma through a new theoretical model. By examining how quark-gluon interactions affect the anisotropic flow of photons, this work provides a way to measure the properties of quark-gluon plasma at a microscopic level. As a result, scientists can use angle-resolved measurements of photon-hadron correlations to investigate the visco-elastic properties of quark-gluon plasma. Furthermore, by comparing the results to existing experiments, such as those at the Large Hadron Collider, this work sets limits on the potential influence of quark-scattering processes on anisotropic flow.

We use numerical simulations to study typical magnetism in lattice structures with triangular and kagome patterns. By simulating various spin models at high temperatures and gradually lowering the temperature, we calculate the magnetization and spin structure factor to identify common magnetic arrangements. For certain interactions in these models, we find a transition from a kagome antiferromagnet to a ferromagnet through an intermediate state with short-range kagome antiferromagnetic correlations. Our results are consistent across different high-temperature starting points, confirming that these magnetic arrangements are typical for specific models in these lattice structures. These findings can be applied to understand typical magnetism in materials with these lattice structures.

A novel method has been devised to manage a dependence structure among multiple binary hypotheses under the overarching framework of the false discovery rate. By creating new, synthesized hypothesis tests based on data transformations of the original tests, the new framework's parameters can be recalculated without requiring individual evaluations of these transformed hypotheses. The method's effectiveness is showcased through the application of it to identify the impact of policy interventions across numerous countries and regions, utilizing large-scale data sets. Furthermore, the method's applicability in other fields, beyond intervention impact identification, is explored using extensive simulations on model assessments, gene expression analysis, and the cross-comparison of deep learning architectures.

This study introduces a simplified model of cosmic expansion, referred to as inflation, to provide new insights into stars and galaxies. This model assumes the universe is expanding at an exponential rate, a premise supported by observations of distant galaxies' redshift, as first noted by Edwin Hubble in 1929. The model provides a more comprehensive explanation for the universe's structure compared to the Big Bang theory, and offers advantages over the steady-state theory in accounting for galaxy evolution. The model derives from the linearity of Hubble's law and explains the relationship between redshift, distance, and the rate of cosmic expansion. The model's implications are further explored through its application to astronomical phenomena, such as the distribution of galaxies and the origin of cosmic microwave background radiation.

The anomaly in the $c\mu$ measurement is successfully explained by the type-X 2HDM's heavy Higgs contributions in a parameter space where $m_h$ and $m_H$ are light and heavy, respectively, with $m_H$ being more than three times the mass of a $W$ boson, thus minimizing its impact on the $g-2$ of a muon. The model's predictions for flavor observables are in agreement with the current best available data.

E-commerce websites often rely on multiple ways to navigate through their extensive product catalogs, and advanced search systems with directed questioning can significantly enhance the search experience by guiding users through a structured inquiry process. However, this approach typically requires pre-defined question sets and can be time-consuming and costly, especially for complex products with many features and options. To address these limitations, we introduce QUICKAR, a pioneering system that utilizes automatic question generation and adapts its questions based on individual user interactions and unique search parameters. By leveraging crowd-sourced information, QUICKAR forms a taxonomy and creates a flexible question network, allowing it to dynamically position concepts and tailor questions to each user's inquiry. We evaluate the system's design and effectiveness through a series of experiments, demonstrating its capabilities and benefits in various scenarios.

Conversational analysis has identified turn-taking as a key feature of dialogue, which is further broken down into coordinated sequences of turns that can either be aligned or distinct. Although previous attempts to identify coordinated sequences relied on pre-defined rules or shallow learning techniques, this research employs unsupervised machine learning to discover dialogue segments that seem to be implicitly defined within conversations. Our study examines three types of features - content, design, and combination - to pinpoint the structural and semantic traits of these hidden segments. By integrating the outputs of deep neural networks and leveraging ensemble learning, we discovered that content and design features perform better than combination features for detecting these hidden segments. Moreover, combining features yields models with the ability to successfully predict the distinct nature of these hidden segments when tested on real-world datasets.

We've developed an open-source visualization tool, RCSEDv2, to display imaging and spectral data. This extension of RCSEDv2v2 enables its users to incorporate additional spectral bands, surpassing the original three bands, RCSEDv1 limitations. RCSEDv2v2 has been deployed on multiple platforms, including Amazon AWS EC2, Google Cloud Platform, and GitHub Pages, allowing it to efficiently process large datasets on both high-performance and low-spec machines. These platforms were utilized for their computational and web-based capabilities, respectively.

A broad range of human activities can be identified and analyzed by temporal action detection and division in video, but traditional approaches relying on large, manually annotated datasets are costly and difficult to scale.  This limitation is addressed by novel self-supervised learning techniques, specifically our proposed Self-supervised Co-occurrence Activity Parsing for Unsupervised Temporal Action Division (SSCAP), which achieves a different direction from similarity-based self-supervision methods by learning a logical relationship-based framework based on the principles of human activities.  This method's pre-training process involves a two-pronged approach combining self-supervised learning and constraint optimization, with the goal of identifying activity segments based on the frequent co-occurrence of related activities.  Our approach demonstrates superior performance compared to top-tier models that depend on labeled data, achieving impressive results across a wide range of diverse action division tasks.

A novel pentaquark state with hidden charm, specifically the SpJ(4430), was recently discovered by Belle II, and we explore its mass spectrum and decay properties through the present algebra. Our analysis reveals two distinct pentaquark states, $PcJ^{\pm}(3055,3070)$ and $PcJ^{\mp}(3065,3085)$, where the $SpJ(4430)$ state sits between them. We predict the mass spectrum of $PcJ^{\mp}(3055\text{--}3085)$ and examine its creation, disintegration, and rebirth in the processes $\bar{D}^{*+}D^{-} \to PcJ(3055\text{--}3085)$. While these states can be directly observed at LHCb, their reconstruction through $\Pi K \bar{K}$ presents significant challenges, and their mass splitting may be too small to resolve at LHCb due to experimental uncertainties.

The increasing importance of Software Testing in industry has created a need for educated professionals capable of designing and analyzing test strategies, creating effective test cases, and interpreting results to take necessary corrective actions. Despite this, a significant disparity exists between the number of graduates with sufficient testing skills and the actual demand for testing professionals. A fundamental aspect of this issue lies in conventional teaching methods, which often rely on conventional lectures and exercises, and may not effectively engage students or foster a deeper understanding of complex concepts. In an effort to address this problem, this study examines the effectiveness of an inquiry-based learning methodology utilizing E-TEA, a web-based system designed to facilitate traditional testing education. By utilizing a quasi-experimental design with two groups of students, one receiving conventional feedback through E-TEA and the other receiving concept-based feedback generated through an inquiry-based approach, the study evaluates the impact of this teaching strategy on two key areas: (1) students' perception of their interest in the course, and (2) their understanding of the material. A comparative analysis of the experimental and control groups' end-of-term exam scores revealed that the experimental group achieved an average score of 16.63, compared to the control group's average score of 15.15, indicating a significant improvement in concept understanding. Furthermore, the experimental results indicate that the conventional interest level of the students remained unchanged.

A major challenge in developing robust machine learning models is mitigating the adverse effects of domain shift during training. Traditional domain adaptation methods typically employ source data with partial labels. However, this approach has two major limitations: the need for access to source data and the involvement of costly labeling. An alternative, source-free domain adaptation, aims to tackle these issues by relying solely on target domain data and the model's weights. A major hurdle in this approach is the lack of access to source data, making theoretical and empirical evaluations difficult due to the impossibility of calculating crucial metrics like maximum inter-cluster distance (MICD) and inter-class angle (ICA). To overcome this limitation, we have devised a theory transfer method, TSDA, which can evaluate the theoretical properties of target clusters, and CLAT, an innovative source-free domain adjustment method that utilizes the transferred theory to align target clusters. Through comprehensive evaluations on 18 datasets from 4 benchmark task types, the proposed method has shown superior performance, with significant improvements of up to 11.6% in accuracy. Furthermore, the theory-based method has also been found to outperform state-of-the-art metrics, demonstrating its effectiveness in accurately representing the theoretical properties of clusters. The code is available for download at https://github.com/leileicai/CLAT_SFDA.

A detailed analysis of gas-core nuclear reactors has been conducted, specifically assessing their suitability as deep space propulsion systems. Two distinct reactor designs were explored: a gaseous core and a liquid-metal-gas core. Notably, these reactors demonstrated exceptional performance characteristics, boasting high power output and elevated burnup levels. However, despite these advantages, gas-core reactors suffer from relatively low fuel density compared to their solid-core counterparts, resulting in decreased specific impulse and overall payload efficiency. The findings indicate that gas-core reactors may not rival other advanced concepts in terms of specific specific impulse and specific mass. The fuel consumption rate for a mission-based trajectory was calculated, revealing that both the gaseous and liquid-metal reactors exhibit similar requirements, which significantly exceed those of the traditional solid-core fission concept.

Neural network-based techniques are increasingly being used in multiple subfields of astrophysics due to their efficiency in analyzing intricate detector signals. Nevertheless, the recent developments in machine learning, specifically deep neural networks, have notably boosted the efficiency and precision of signal analysis in various tasks. Despite these advancements, the complexity of these networks often results in poor generalization and local overfitting, which can be problematic. To address these shortcomings, this study investigates the integration of domain-specific knowledge in neural network designs to tackle these limitations. We leverage transfer learning and incorporate wavelet transforms into the domain-adaptation approach, which allows for leveraging expertise from related particle shower localization problems and transforming signal distributions to make them more conducive to neural network training. Through our experimental evaluation, we observed significant improvements, specifically ~10% higher precision compared to conventional convolutional neural networks, albeit at the expense of slightly higher computational requirements.

As interest in characterizing exoplanet atmospheres grows, precise cross-section data for various molecules is crucial. Unfortunately, the scope of cross-section data available so far has primarily focused on exoplanets near their host stars. In contrast, the atmospheres of substellar objects, including brown dwarfs and giant planets, require accurate data despite being less accessible due to their lower signal strength. Notably, the cross-section data available for these substellar environments is currently insufficient. In response to this gap, the cross-section database EXOPLINES has been created to facilitate research on the atmospheric composition of substellar objects. The database encompasses absorption cross-sections, line lists, and molecular absorption cross-sections for key molecules such as H2O, CH4, NH3, and CO2, enabling researchers to accurately model the spectra of substellar objects.

The process of grounding forms a fundamental aspect of answer set computation for logic programs.  Current approaches to grounding rely on a strict limit on recursive program rules that can't reference answer set variables multiple times within a single rule. 逾越 this strict limit allows for more comprehensive modeling of real-world problems.  Recent advancements in grounding technology have expanded the range of problems that can be effectively grounded.  Three key principles underpin the complexity of grounding: the ability to interpret program symbols, the capacity to process variables and their bindings, and the ability to understand logical connectives.  Symmetry in ground programs is another crucial aspect that can impact the complexity of grounding, particularly with the introduction of NEMs (Non-Equivalence Matrix Annihilation Operators).  A systematic framework has been proposed to analyze the complexity of grounding based on these principles and symmetries.  This framework helps to understand the complexity of grounding and identify areas for potential improvement.

One fundamental principle in physics is the conservation of energy, which is a direct consequence of time's symmetry. In generalized quantum theories, no such link exists between quantum counterparts and their basic axioms. We have derived a novel principle rooted in the preservation of quantum channel norm, which is associated with a key assumption regarding the displacement of a quantum system over time. This assumption is demonstrated to be a direct reflection of time's continuous and uniform progression. Our findings enable the construction of a practical quantum clock that can measure the system's evolution.

In multidimensional time series models with non-stationary characteristics, we investigate robust-tailed, non-stationary models featuring non-stationary GARCH and stochastic volatility components. We develop a new method to estimate these models using weighted least squares estimation methods. Our research reveals that our estimators have a specific property of consistency and asymptotic normality, even when the model components have infinite variance. To address computational difficulties, we create a multi-step estimator that involves infinite variance components with infinite variance. Furthermore, we provide an example of applying our new approach to actual data.

Quantum error correction is a critical aspect of quantum computation. Low-density parity-check error correction codes are currently under significant investigation due to their capacity to offer efficient error correction for large quantities of quantum data stored in quantum memory. However, current LDPC code designs have a drawback in that they require a lengthy interaction time, making them susceptible to time-based errors. In this research, a new LDPC code, the complete graph code (GRC), has been developed to address this limitation while maintaining strong error correction performance for all noise models and link failure scenarios. The GRC's check operators are organized into repeated blocks that are accessed in a round-robin manner, significantly shortening the error correction duration to a small fixed number of time intervals that does not increase with the system's size. Simulation results show that for qubit loss and depolarizing noise, GRC can achieve a logical error rate below unity for practical parameter values, significantly outperforming existing codes in terms of efficiency and speed.

In graph theory, a dominating ensemble is a way to represent dominating sets as a distribution. We propose a method called Sampled Domination, a distributed algorithm that calculates a distance-r dominating ensemble within O(r^2 log n) steps with high probability. We present a new model of high-performance distributed computation. Sampled Domination operates efficiently on high-girth graphs with large degrees, achieving a different result than a previous algorithm called Local Computation, which only worked for small values of r and had lower time complexity, but required higher average vertex degrees.

We are conducting an in-depth examination of the mass-boundary correspondence principle in disordered insulators with elevated topological characteristics. Specifically, adding a mass perturbation to a two-dimensional theta vacuum in the theta insulator model in space-time results in an anomalous boundary current in response to an external electromagnetic field, an effect that changes in proportion to the perturbation strength. Consequently, strong topological insulators with disorder can remain in their topological state even when exposed to significant mass perturbations, resulting in boundary states that exhibit lower symmetry due to the absence of time-reversal invariance. Utilizing the replica trick in computational studies, we observe that phase transitions resulting from mass perturbations are correlated with changes in boundary behavior, where the vanishing of bulk topological markers coincides with delocalized states emerging from the boundary Hamiltonian. Our findings, particularly the observed bound-transport correspondence, offer valuable insights for the effective manipulation of boundary currents on theta vacuums through mass perturbations.

Recent searches for heavy neutral particles in proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV utilize various decay pathways of chargino-neutralino pairs and two Z bosons, both accompanied by jets. These searches rely on the METJet and Dijet event topologies and employ sophisticated background estimation techniques and signal extraction methods such as sidebands and control regions. Inadvertently, these analyses also constrain supersymmetry mass models and exclude various mass combinations for neutralino and chargino models, notably models like m0MSTHug and mX2MSSM with specific mass configurations for m_1/2, m_{\tilde{\tau}^*}, m_{\tilde{\mu}^*}, and m_{\tilde{\nu}_\tau,\tilde{\mu}}.

A 3D camera pose allows for a bird's-eye view of the world through photorealistic 3D content, with photometric neural rendering achieving remarkable results. Nevertheless, a significant drawback is its computational intensity, primarily due to a multi-pass process. Researchers propose the introduction of brightness field neural rendering as a more efficient solution, reducing the process to a single pass. They introduce the concept of brightness field neural rendering as the key innovation, allowing for the direct use of a smaller, low-resolution query renderer without impacting visual quality. To further optimize rendering time, a caching technique is employed to process similar queries only once. The proposed system, known as Brightness Field Neural Rendering, results in a significant time reduction of more than 10 times, all while maintaining visual quality comparable to the original method. The implementation of brightness field neural rendering also allows for the creation of interactive 3D views of complex scenes, such as those captured from high-resolution cameras.

Observations conducted at the SOAR telescope in 2020 along with previously unpublished data, yielded a dataset of 1,745 measurements involving 288 target stars and a companion of nine binary systems. The successful collection of this dataset relied on the implementation of a newly designed, digitally controlled phase mask and an upgraded speckle imaging camera, designed and built by the IAC and the University of Arizona. The new phase mask, utilizing 8 masks per frame, enabled more accurate speckle measurements, enhancing the system's capability to achieve high-resolution imaging, a capability that was rigorously tested using calibration sources and numerous scientific targets. The performance of this phase mask was evaluated through a thorough analysis of its impact on binary discovery rates within the SOAR dataset, revealing significant improvements in its detection capabilities. The SOAR telescope's imaging capabilities allowed for the precise measurement of binary systems spanning a wide range of angular separations, from a few to over 1 arcsecond, and facilitated the determination of their masses. Furthermore, the telescope's capabilities enabled more accurate photometric measurements of primary systems, yielding a precision of approximately 0.015 magnitudes per frame, enhancing our understanding of various celestial objects. Overall, the SOAR dataset of 2020 contributed valuable insights to our knowledge of binary systems, providing essential constraints for their physical properties and evolutionary stages.

We establish a method to build a multicharge, multispin species of the automorphic sheaf associated with a derived category of motivic sheaves originally conceived for chialgebras attached to a reductive group. Our findings reveal that the cosmic chiral algebras exhibit a duality between color and kinematics, and we establish a connection with the motivic sheaf approach. We further extend this approach to the case of chiral algebras related to Kosmann-Buisson algebras, and adapt the cosmic chiral algebra concept to derived categories pertinent to the theory of elliptic nets. Our study incorporates supplementary theory on chiral algebras and chiral cohomology. Building on this framework, we integrate Gaudin models and quantum integrable systems research to broaden cosmic chiral algebra concepts and connect with existing literature on quantum integrable systems.

A long-duration solar flare, specifically AR12673 on May 4, 2011, produced a particularly notable type of radio burst known as a Type III burst, observed by the low-frequency LOFAR telescope. The telescope detected strong radio signals at frequencies below 165 MHz, indicating interaction between plasma and magnetic fields driven by the piston surge phenomenon at extremely low altitudes. The research revealed that this event occurred at altitudes of less than 2 solar radii, suggesting a novel understanding of piston surge interactions within the low solar corona, an area that has traditionally been challenging to study.

In the general two Higgs doublet model with modified Yukawa interactions, we have derived a probability examination to rule out flavor anomalies as a valid explanation. With nearly complete exclusion probabilities of over 95% in the individual regions of the $2-3$ and $3-3-3$ sectors, as well as the second and third generation up-type Yukawa sector, this model has been heavily constrained in an attempt to accommodate flavor anomalies and the muon's magnetic dipole moment discrepancies in a type II two Higgs doublet model.

This study explores the dynamics of a single particle moving within a fluid influenced by randomly changing forces. The article focuses on particles within a swirling fluid model, where the change in force is represented by a multi-dimensional Weierstrass function with randomly placed frequencies to simulate the fluid's behavior. By building on the results of previous research, we establish the continuity and self-similarity of particle paths under the influence of these randomly changing forces. The article also investigates the properties of particle paths under the influence of two specific examples of this fluid model.

The calculation of reduced density matrices and entanglement measures for specific systems is a widely used method for analyzing complete state vectors via Schur-Weyl duality, particularly in contexts involving boson sampling. However, this approach has a significant drawback: it necessitates solving an exponential scaling problem with system size. Researchers in [related paper] found a way to bypass this bottleneck by identifying a simplified, polynomial-scaling criterion for determining when two modes are not entangled. Building on this insight, they extended its application to scenarios involving many modes and various partitions. To achieve this, they introduced an analytical measure of entanglement that grows polynomially with mode number, effectively addressing the associated exponential complexity issue.

Temporally organized data from 1,000 to 10,000 variables is becoming more accessible in life sciences, presenting both opportunities and challenges. The problems associated with time series analysis, however, are compounded by issues such as limited sample sizes and the absence of clear labels. To address these difficulties, we suggest a two-pronged approach: employing a generative model and incorporating external labels obtained through a stepwise process. Our method involves learning a time-series distribution that can generate synthetic data and a predictive label estimator tailored to the individual data distribution. To enhance label acquisition, we developed a technique for measuring relevance and incorporating labels into the model through classification labels obtained from external labels. Our model achieved notable results when tested on three biological datasets and significantly surpassed current state-of-the-art approaches.

We examine the extent to which a finite-state system with partially observable components can be predicted using different types of neural networks, specifically focusing on the necessity of hidden, dynamic state representations for effective operation. In the absence of full environmental awareness, recurrent architectures, which incorporate memory and allow for future prediction, become essential for achieving optimal performance. We categorize such systems into two groups based on their complexity: a simpler class that can be successfully managed by a particular type of feedback mechanism and a more intricate class requiring more advanced structures. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our analysis by applying it to two specific scenarios: a system involving random transitions and another based on the mixing of signal frequencies.

The majority of research in action detection relies heavily on fully annotated datasets, which are time-consuming and labor-intensive to prepare. To address this issue, there has been a growing interest in developing weakly-annotated action detection techniques utilizing graph convolutional networks (GCNs). In this area, we suggest an innovative weakly-annotated action detection technique centered around GCNs that enhances the model's ability to choose detection points based on spatial relationships. To achieve this, we introduce a new spatial relationship descriptor along with dynamic graph construction methods to boost graph convolution processing. To further refine our method's performance at making predictions, we propose combining hierarchical detection with spatial relationship descriptors and encapsulating them within a hierarchical attention framework. Extensive experiments conducted on THES-1K, Kinetics, UCF101, UC100, and JHMDB datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms previously established benchmarks in context-aware action detection.

The 2021 Image Reliability Challenge focused on evaluating deep neural networks for visual tasks, with participants developing and submitting networks to detect subtle differences between real and synthetic images. Six participants proposed new methods or enhanced existing ones and used ensemble strategies to achieve superior performance. Participants also reported several important findings, including the importance of using appropriate training data and appropriate assessment methods.

This report focuses on the long-term dynamics of two types of perturbations in parabolic equations whose unperturbed forms have uniform but degenerating diffusion and singular noise when the domain is unbounded and a boundary condition is applied. Specifically, we investigate: 1) the impact of a boundary layer on the dynamics when a weak drift is introduced, and 2) the long-term effects of rapidly oscillating noise on partial differential equations (PDPs) in heterogeneous environments. Our analysis reveals that while perturbation 1 leads to a boundary layer formation, perturbation 2 results in a homogenization-driven metastable behavior, under specific conditions. Homogenization refers to the process of rapidly changing details of a medium to produce an averaged, homogeneous model. The reported findings provide a comprehensive analysis of these two types of perturbations, covering various aspects such as their existence, stability, and the conditions under which they hold true. The analysis employs a combination of probabilistic and analytical methods to achieve these results. Notably, we also demonstrate the implications of these perturbations on the associated stochastic processes.

The nuclear substance is analyzed within a magnetized environment by using the second-order perturbation theory based on the correlated hypernetted-chain equation of state. This involves calculating the correlation potentials of nuclear systems with and without an intense magnetic field. To achieve this, the potential of the magnetic field is considered as a perturbation, and the correlated hypernetted-chain equation of state is used to account for nuclear correlations. Calculations are based on a nuclear system in the absence of center-of-mass motion and employ the LOCV method with a nuclear interaction that includes a Jastrow correlation factor and the Argonne v14 two-body potential. This study finds that the magnetic field's perturbation effect on nuclear system substance is negligible compared to a system without a magnetic field. This suggests that the nuclear system has minimal response to an intense magnetic field. This study's findings are comparable to those of neutron matter in a magnetized environment.

Machine learning models' accuracy can be compromised by privacy breaches within training datasets. This issue becomes particularly significant in scenarios where communication between a central server and clients is limited due to bandwidth constraints. To address this challenge, a novel federated learning approach called $\DP$-$REC$ has been developed. This method employs differential privacy to safeguard the security of information exchanged between the central server and clients. To mitigate communication costs, the $\DP$-$REC$ technique utilizes compressed data transmission for both the server-to-client and client-to-server communication cycles. Our research evaluates the performance of $\DP$-$REC$ through experiments on real-world university student datasets. The results demonstrate that $\DP$-$REC$ achieves superior performance compared to existing federated learning methods while providing enhanced security for education-related applications.

A star formation ensemble in the northern sky has garnered attention due to its resemblance to nearby star clusters like those in the southern sky, where an unusual lack of free-floating planets is observed. By examining UV images of this ensemble, we discovered that a previously unknown cloud, later identified as part of the Lupus complex, contains an area known as L1641, home to the star-forming region L1688, which includes IC348. Further research revealed the presence of a distant, star-forming region called L1544 within this area. A new star cluster, IC5058, was also discovered, containing about 150 stars, with its primary star being a massive A-type star called IC5058 A, along with a fainter, nearby, star.

Current optical character recognition systems produce inaccurate results when processing complex tables in PDF documents, particularly due to their inability to recognize empty cells and their restrictive use of character-level encodings. The structure of these tables is critical for understanding and revealing context-dependent relationships. In an effort to overcome these limitations, we developed a novel graph neural network architecture, along with an innovative representation encoding technique, that leverages table structure to enhance accuracy. The resulting improvements in table retrieval are substantial, surpassing existing state-of-the-art systems by 10-15% based on our experiments using annotated documents containing 2,500 tables from three diverse domains.

In complex, incomplete games involving human agents with distinct cognitive structures, we employ logical LPEs to model the structures. We provide a comprehensive characterization of incomplete knowledge within the context of logical LPEs, mirroring the properties of S5-logical equivalence. Furthermore, we establish a significant outcome for intransitive or incomplete relations among the 2LPE models associated with each agent, indicating that such restrictions guarantee the existence of a pure Nash equilibrium. We illustrate our findings with a case study of a two-phase market-entry game.

This study introduces the concept of Autonomous Population Assessment, a survey technique proposed to enhance survey efficiency and reduce costs while maintaining survey quality. In countries with extensive, inaccessible road networks, populations are notoriously difficult to accurately gauge due to the prohibitively expensive cost of conducting door-to-door surveys. As a potential solution, AAPA utilizes drone-captured imagery to identify road networks and allocates images strategically across estimated population centers. Following this, cross-validation techniques are employed to refine road mapping and refine the detection of inhabited areas, ultimately allowing for image removal in low-residence areas and the identification of a suitable sample for human enumeration. In nations like Mozambique, which lack reliable road networks, this approach could facilitate direct surveys of inaccessible populations. A preliminary evaluation of this method in Mozambique has shown promising outcomes in terms of direct survey efficiency and overall costs.

Over the past ten years, data analysis techniques utilizing artificially created negative examples, known as cold data, have gained significant attention due to their ability to enhance machine learning algorithms' efficiency and accuracy in classification tasks, often referred to as cold war classification. This research introduces a new method for creating such filters that are only capable of producing false positive results. We also present an improved algorithm for existing techniques, specifically the Count Min Sketch, which is shown to outperform them by as much as 40%. An empirical study was conducted to verify the benefits of our approach in a specific scenario involving the evaluation of course recommendation systems, and this approach was found to be effective in reducing computation time.

To grasp both static and dynamic properties of quantum fluids of variable spin, it is crucial to transform between particles and molecules. While the static spin-molecule transformation through Feshbach resonance has been widely studied, its dynamic counterpart remains largely unexplored. We've demonstrated that rapid spin-m transformation can be achieved through coherent manipulation of spin states and Mott insulating configurations. By initially inducing a Mott insulator and then applying a magnetic field, we've observed a superfluid emergence within the interval of finite feshbach molecules' binding energy. This result signifies a genuine and swift conversion of spin to variable spin configuration and holds potential implications for the fabrication of quantum circuits, spin qubit manipulation, and ultrafast spin-based device development.

A novel multi-scale SPH method is introduced for solving complex multi-phase fluid-structure interaction problems. This approach employs a high-resolution SPH solver to simulate fluid dynamics and a coarser solver, coupled with an arbitrary Lagrangian-Eulerian method, to simulate structural dynamics, effectively improving computational efficiency. Numerical experiments demonstrate that this method preserves numerical stability and conservation properties, while also achieving significant speed-ups in solving fluid-structure interaction and bubble dynamics problems compared to a standard single-scale solver.

As machine learning continues to advance, it is being applied to an ever-growing number of fields, but the growing complexity of datasets poses a significant challenge. There are currently no established models capable of addressing the inherent difficulties associated with these datasets, prompting the need for new approaches. One potential solution is quantum machine learning, which has gained considerable interest in recent years. In the context of this research, we introduced and examined a framework called quantum unmonitored learning (QUML), which enables data to be stored in a quantum memory device without requiring monitoring. Furthermore, we also considered a type of quantum machine learning (QL) that involves monitoring the quantum memory device, which we referred to as quantum monitored learning (QML). In our experiments, we evaluated the effectiveness of the proposed QUML, QML, and the previously established quantum least squares (QLS) model by applying them to real-world datasets. Notably, we demonstrated that QUML and QML outperformed QLS in terms of accuracy and computational efficiency for both unstructured and structured data, with the QML framework even being able to achieve quality results in a reduced number of training iterations. In our experiments using a superconducting quantum processor, we measured the accuracy of QUML and QML by training the model in up to 12 qubits, which significantly improved its performance in comparison to QLS.

A recent text-to-speech algorithm called FastPitch excels in intonation,
duration, and timbre synthesis while needing minimal training data due to its
disentangled encoding scheme of pitch, timbre, and text. Nonetheless, during
inference its cross-spectral prediction may yield unsuitable acoustic results.
This research presents a conditional pitch augmenerator to suggest plausible
pitch patterns that maintain timbre integrity and subsequently incorporates
these probabilities via a reinforcement learning process to maintain optimal
speech quality. Experiments indicate a voice-quality decrease of less than one
point on the mean opinion score scale and significantly reduce word error rates
in automatic speech recognition tasks. Notably, our method decreases pitch
distortion by more than 80% and enhances speech intonation.

This research introduces a model, named Hopper, for addressing short and long-term traffic forecasting challenges across various settings, including singular scenarios and urban areas comprising multiple sites. Hopper is a multi-hop transformer architecture that generates predicted traffic patterns based on past traffic timeseries data and dynamic sensor locations like weather or roadwork schedules. Hopper efficiently identifies distant and temporally widespread patterns using multiple mechanisms including self-attention and spatial modules, and further refines predictions with temporal modules that capture temporal patterns. Hopper outperforms existing approaches on a singular dataset (PEMS-03) and significantly surpasses other methods, including simple baselines, on two larger datasets (PEMS-09 and PEMS-04) and handles various inference tasks.

Physicists created a precise measurement of the W boson mass by analyzing numerous collisions between protons at a record-breaking energy of 13 TeV, where 35.8 inverse femtobarns of data were collected. To arrive at their results, the researchers employed simulated data to correct their findings for more accurate outcomes using a technique called an optimal likelihood fit. Their results showed a lepton mass of approximately 30.97 GeV/c^2 with significantly high statistical accuracy.

The rapid advancement of Telepresence Robot Control (TROC) technologies has greatly benefited both the military and civilian sectors, enabling users to remotely control robots in hazardous environments, such as war zones and disaster relief sites, where human presence is either impractical or dangerous. As TROC technology continues to evolve, there's a growing need for a user-friendly evaluation method to assess the Quality of Experience (QoE) for this type of service. Current QoE assessment methods, which are either not interactive or only partially interactive, have several limitations. They fail to simulate real-world scenarios, such as a user being unable to see an obstacle due to a lack of video quality, which could lead to the robot crashing into the obstacle. To address this issue, we propose an interactive QoE assessment method for TROC that allows for a more accurate simulation of real-world scenarios and more accurate QoE assessments. We also present an initial study on the proposed approach and provide a website demonstrating the practical application of this method.

This study introduces Bayesian hierarchical linear forecasting models as a tool to mitigate overfitting in statistical learning techniques by incorporating prior knowledge about model parameters in parameter estimation. Building upon these models, we develop methods to adaptively estimate prior hyperparameters based on model data, thereby maintaining model flexibility. Our analysis examines forecasting performance in terms of mean squared error for hierarchical linear models, particularly in a random effects setting with a non-informative prior for the error, demonstrating that a Bayesian model can outperform traditional linear models in terms of forecast accuracy. We provide an illustrative empirical evaluation of our approach to achieving improved forecasting performance.

To explore the game of Mafia, a numerical model was developed, which is capable of simulating various scenarios. By utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, probabilities of different outcomes in a mafia game with a given number of citizens, detectives, and mafia members, as well as the probability of mafia detection and detection method, can be calculated. We applied and expanded upon these findings by modeling a variation of Mafia known as "Blood Mafia," which adds a shooter to the game. This variation allows players to eliminate any player of their choice, with knowledge of their opponent's identity obtained through a specific game mechanic. Monte Carlo simulations were used to extend the original model and analyze multiple scenarios of this new game variant.

In the paper, the influence of concurrent gas accumulation onto two large planets is examined through three-dimensional simulations of a protoplanetary disk. The simulations show that gas can be channelled by vortices, concentrating material within the disk's midplane, where the vortices reside. A possible scenario is that two large planets are associated with stable, adjacent vortices, channeling gas onto themselves and simultaneously influencing the disk's visibility in certain wavelengths. The study demonstrates that gas accretion onto these planets occurs faster when it is supplied from the surrounding disk in a focused manner by the vortices than from the more conventional accretion rates typically assumed. Moreover, the study reveals that a significant portion of the gas supplied can be expelled from the planets' equatorial regions back into the disk due to centrifugal forces, potentially contributing to disk replenishment. The findings of this research have significant implications for the understanding of giant planets' formation and the evolution of their disks.

In amorphous silicon films, intertube transport, which, is typically blocked by insulation, exhibits conductive behavior due to vibrations transmitted between tubes through sound waves. This conductive behavior surpasses that of 1D interaction limits and can be better described by a model of sound-wave-like particle interactions. At low temperatures, intertube conductance in a film of single-layer nanotubes is minimal, but at higher temperatures, it is significantly increased due to these vibrations. Notably, the intertube conductance in a film of nanotubes is higher than that of individual nanotubes measured using a two-terminal setup.

This paper proposes a novel approach to fuzzy k-means clustering that addresses two key limitations of the traditional method when dealing with high-dimensional data. To combat the curse of dimensionality, each data point is assigned a unique set of weights based on its specific dimension, which are derived from maximizing the probability distribution of dimension weights within the dataset. By incorporating weighted dimensions data, the algorithm minimizes a modified cost function. To optimize the traditional cost function and prevent getting stuck in local optima, the paper also introduces a stochastic initialization method for cluster centers. The effectiveness of our method is validated through its comparison with two existing algorithms on a dataset of 138,000 customers at a major online retailer.

Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) models have been successfully implemented in numerous scenarios, combining the benefits of simplicity and efficiency. Nevertheless, the application of MoE in non-convex optimization problems has encountered significant challenges, with the convergence issue being particularly difficult to resolve. As a result, the design of efficient algorithms for MoE remains an ongoing area of study. This paper introduces a range of steady and efficient algorithms for MoE models that overcome existing moe gates. Specifically, the proposed algorithms not only guarantee convergence to at least one optimal solution, but also ensure that a gate's output remains bounded, facilitating connection to a standard non-convex optimization model. Furthermore, this paper investigates a variety of scenarios, demonstrating the effectiveness of these new algorithms, including convex and non-convex MoE settings, a specific scenario illustrating steady gate performance, and a comparison with a standard gate implementation, highlighting notable efficiency benefits. A comprehensive analysis of these algorithms on real-world datasets is presented, utilizing a variety of experimental settings.

Consider a hyperbolic surface of a specific genus accompanied by two special points. By examining the possible ways to connect these points through token movements, a certain type of quotient surface emerges, genus of which depends on the surface's genus. The study focuses on three-related surfaces and their Jacobians, belonging to a certain family obtained through a continuous transformation process of gluing. The choice of a particular line bundle on the Jacobian yields a genus-two abelian variety known as a Prym variety through decomposition. For each transformation, there is an associated token-firing game, based on graph properties of the corresponding surface. An important conjecture proposes a continuity property for a specific invariant related to these Prym varieties, connected to movement of special points on the respective surfaces.

A method is proposed for detecting the effects of beyond-Standard-Model physics on the polarization of distant astrophysical sources. This involves a 'cosmic birefringence' effect where linearly polarized light has its polarization angle rotated during its journey through space due to its parity-violating interactions with new physics. Observations on relatively nearby sources, such as galaxies and the CMB, have established that, on a global scale, birefringence cannot exceed approximately $0.3$ rad without creating observable distortions or anomalies. This implies a stringent constraint on the parity-violating B-field, being less than or comparable to the Planck scale. Furthermore, birefringence could offer insight into the energy scale of the unknown physics, particularly in scenarios where the rotation angle is linked to the vacuum expectation value of a new scalar field related to dark energy. In such a scenario, a non-zero birefringence would necessitate a scalar field vacuum expectation significantly smaller than the Planck scale, around 20 times higher than that of Higgs's.

Our research presents new findings from far ultraviolet observations of the globular cluster NGC 4147. Using four UVIT images, 28 blue horizontal branch stars with potential blue straggler classification were discovered. Three pairs of BHB stars, however, showed the UBV color and magnitude dispersion expected for regular BHB stars. In addition, we report the detection of a previously unaccounted for blue straggler star located on the main sequence within the cluster.

Given a family of smooth projective varieties with a boundary, and a compactification that includes a divisor with irreducible components, we investigate the impact of the compactification on the family's cohomology groups, specifically for a particular cohomology group where the components have a small individual impact, we demonstrate that the cohomology groups vary continuously, thus validating a localized version of the Mumford-Hartshorne conjecture's principle. This is achieved by incorporating a study of D-modules that focuses on a particular type of unipotent monodromy.

Deep neural networks have become increasingly prevalent due to their remarkable capability of learning and generalizing from data they've never encountered before. The concept of transferability, which is often assumed to be universal and context-independent, is being examined more closely in this research. The study identifies two primary principles of transferability: the applicability of pre-trained models across various domains without adjustment, and the non-superiority of specialized models compared to general-purpose ones in tasks involving multiple domains. However, these principles are shown to be contingent upon data volume and distribution within the target domain. Through theoretical analysis, this research provides clarity on the limitations and scope of these principles. The study also discusses how targeting a specific domain can be more effective in certain scenarios and emphasizes the value of modeling target domain data characteristics in improving transferability. The discussion is supported by a simple statistical model that takes into account domain-specific data correlations and showcases the benefits of incorporating this knowledge in the learning process.

In various systems, the spread of information is a critical process, and its speed is influenced by the way networks are organized into modules. Researchers have explored the connection between information propagation and modular structures in networks, focusing on how a measure called the "information discrepancy" reveals the spread of information and helps determine the effective speed of information dissemination. By analyzing this relationship across different types of networks with varying levels of modularity and a real-world network of scientific collaborations, they found that highly modular networks facilitate faster information spread than random化的同等密度网络. Moreover, a linear relationship exists between information discrepancy and modularity, allowing for an explanation of how information moves through networks. Interestingly, moderate levels of modularity were optimal for spreading information, demonstrating the importance of network structure in shaping information flow.

Using Thomas-Yau volume entropy, we obtain distinctiveness quantities for two families of metrics on the space of two-dimensional surfaces. The first family, consisting of uniquely solitons, allows us to establish lower bounds for the dimension of the moduli space of 2-dimensional area-area map conical singularities. The second family, made up of Hermitian metrics derived from Higgs bundles via the Hitchin equation, provides lower bounds for the rank of the flag and torus potential map. We complement this with observations on the distance function and Hessian, focusing on the flaring effect along gradient lines in the moduli space of types A and B metrics.

A mathematical framework known as the Standard Perturbation Model accurately describes how light travels through optical networks when influenced by minor irregularities. Although it has been extensively used for decades, it's still not clear how well this model works for individual unamplified links in realistic settings. We examined how well the model approximates actual signal behavior in such links and found that for small disruptions, it provides an 80% accurate representation of the link's characteristics. However, as disruptions grow larger, its accuracy decreases. We developed a new approach called the enhanced perturbation model, which improves upon it by considering how the frequency of the light signal affects its propagation. We found that for large disruptions, this improved model achieves an 80% accuracy and, as disruptions become very small, it closely matches model C in cases of weak disruptions, but differs significantly in cases of strong disruptions.

In recent years, mobile phones have become a focal point for researchers, 
who are constantly at odds with exploit developers, whose innovations in 
zero-day vulnerabilities have led to the creation of novel exploitation 
techniques. Building on this backdrop, this paper examines the most influential 
research on Issue-Space Evasion assaults, a category of exploits that involve 
bypassing security measures by leveraging non-traditional attack vectors. 
These exploits, primarily targeting the Android platform, have relied on 
established security flaws such as buffer overflows and buffer overflows with 
offsets. Given the rapidly evolving nature of exploitation techniques, this 
paper serves as a valuable resource for contemporary researchers, despite being 
based on earlier work.

Distributed computing systems, despite being cost-effective and scalable alternatives, come with the challenge of dealing with the complexities associated with resource heterogeneity, fault tolerance, and security concerns. The Ozy distributed runtime platform, which initially focused on transparent and efficient grid computing for scientific data, has undergone significant improvements to become a more versatile and scalable runtime system capable of supporting various distributed applications.
